query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a low weight fraction of copper‐coated graphene (Cu@Gr) directly into the starting W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation during sintering and subsequent thermal/irradiation service, leading to a more continuous Cu network and enhanced thermal conductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite having tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments dispersed in a copper matrix, processed by conventional methods that produce phase separation and voids at the W–Cu interfaces.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small amount (~0.8 wt.%) of copper‐coated graphene uniformly into the composite powder mixture before sintering, so that it is integrated during densification (for example, by spark plasma sintering).
generation.conditions: The intervention is implemented during the sintering process (e.g., SPS at 1280 °C, 30 MPa for ~10 min) and is aimed at composites used under high heat-transfer loads and irradiation exposure, such as in joints between tungsten-based plasma-facing components and copper-based cooling structures.
generation.structural_mediator: The Cu@Gr additive promotes formation of an enhanced three-dimensional interconnected Cu network with improved interfacial bonding and reduced voids between W and Cu phases.
generation.mechanism: Copper‐coated graphene acts as an activator for sintering by increasing grain-boundary diffusivity and improving the wettability of copper with tungsten. This enables more effective liquid Cu infiltration while concurrently limiting copper evaporation and dewetting. The graphene also serves as a physical barrier against interfacial reactions (e.g., carbide formation) that can exacerbate phase separation, thereby stabilizing the microstructure under heat load and irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated composite, the Cu@Gr-doped composite is predicted to exhibit a notably denser microstructure with fewer interfacial voids and a more uniform, continuous Cu network. This microstructural improvement should translate to an increase in thermal conductivity (on the order of approximately 20–25% higher, consistent with improvements observed in related systems) under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite processed under analogous sintering conditions that suffers from phase separation and interfacial void formation, leading to inferior thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to composites fabricated via powder metallurgy/SPS at high temperatures (near or above the melting point of Cu) under moderate pressures, and its anticipated benefits are relevant specifically for applications involving cyclic high heat flux and moderate irradiation typical of plasma-facing/cooling component interfaces.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the results of PMC5736653 (which demonstrated that Cu@Gr additives improve electrical and thermal properties through enhanced Cu network formation and inhibited carbide formation) to the specific challenge of phase separation and interfacial voids observed in conventional high-temperature sintering (as discussed in PMC12028711). Uncertainty remains over the long-term stability of the graphene-modified interfaces under prolonged irradiation and thermal cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite joints using identical powder mixtures and sintering conditions (e.g., SPS at 1280 °C, 30 MPa for 10 min): one set incorporating ~0.8 wt.% Cu@Gr and one undoped control. Subject both sets to accelerated heat-transfer cycling and controlled irradiation (using, for example, ion bombardment to simulate plasma conditions). After processing and post-service simulation, perform detailed microstructural analysis (via SEM/EDS) to assess interfacial void formation and phase distribution, and measure thermal conductivity.
measurements: Thermal conductivity of the composites pre- and post-service simulation
Microstructural characterization of W–Cu interfaces (quantitative porosity and void analysis)
Electrical conductivity (as a proxy for network continuity)
Irradiation-induced swelling or phase stability indicators
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu@Gr-doped composites do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial voids or phase separation and no corresponding enhancement in thermal conductivity relative to the undoped baseline (within experimental error), then the hypothesis is falsified.
